current_criteria.name: temporal_consistency
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s claim about motion, state change, or sequence is visually plausible or inferable from the image — only when such a claim is explicitly or implicitly implied by the question or visual context. It does NOT apply to static scenes (where no motion or state change is implied) or to answers that make no temporal claims (e.g., ‘a red cup’). The criterion is strictly inapplicable if neither candidate answer contains a temporal claim. Visual plausibility includes reasonable inferences from posture, trajectory, occlusion, motion blur, or contextual cues — e.g., ‘the cat is running’ if posture implies motion, or ‘the door is swinging open’ if trajectory suggests movement. The criterion does NOT penalize plausible motion inferences — only explicit contradictions (e.g., ‘walking’ with planted feet, ‘falling’ with no downward trajectory). Temporal claims that infer time (e.g., ‘recently’, ‘just’, ‘before’) are explicitly excluded — evaluation is limited to motion, state change, or sequence. If both answers are factually correct, preference is given to the answer with the most visually supported temporal claim — but only if both make temporal claims. Workers must first verify factual correctness under ‘factual_consistency’ — then, if both answers are factually correct and contain temporal claims, apply this criterion. If one answer is hallucinated or factually incorrect, it is disqualified — and the criterion is inapplicable. Visual evidence must support the temporal claim — not speculative or inferred claims without visual grounding. A claim is ‘visually supported’ if it is either directly visible (e.g., motion blur, trajectory) or inferable from visual structure (e.g., posture suggesting motion, occlusion implying depth change). This criterion must not be used to evaluate factual accuracy — only to compare temporal plausibility among factually correct temporal claims.
